expectations.description: Recommends ICC over Cohen's kappa for this case (continuous/ordinal ratings, not pure categorical)
expectations.evidence: Opens with 'Use ICC, not Cohen's kappa' and provides clear rationale for a 5-point ordinal severity scale

expectations.description: Mentions that Cohen's kappa is for categorical agreement, while ICC is for continuous reliability
expectations.evidence: States 'Cohen's kappa is a measure of categorical agreement — it's designed for nominal or coarsely categorical ratings' and contrasts with ICC for ordinal/continuous scales

expectations.description: Mentions that there are multiple ICC variants (Shrout & Fleiss labels 1/2/3 OR McGraw-Wong A/C, single vs. average)
expectations.evidence: Lists ICC(1,1), ICC(2,1), ICC(3,1) with Shrout & Fleiss labels and references McGraw & Wong (1996) ICC(A,1) notation

expectations.description: Recommends a specific ICC type with rationale (e.g., ICC(2,1) absolute agreement if generalizing to other clinicians)
expectations.evidence: Recommends 'ICC(2,1) with absolute agreement' with explicit rationale: 'you likely want results to generalize to other clinicians like these two'

expectations.description: Distinguishes between absolute agreement and consistency, OR between single-rater and average-rater ICC
expectations.evidence: Explicitly distinguishes absolute agreement vs. consistency and single-measure ICC(2,1) vs. average-measure ICC(2,k)

expectations.description: Mentions psych::ICC() or a comparable function
expectations.evidence: Provides R code block using psych::ICC(rating_matrix) with explanation

expectations.description: Optionally mentions that for ordinal data weighted kappa is an alternative if you want kappa specifically
expectations.evidence: States 'If you're committed to a kappa-family statistic, weighted kappa — with linear or quadratic weights — at least acknowledges the ordinal structure'
